title: That time six Navy aircraft vanished without a trace in the Bermuda Triangle
excerpt: The U.S. Navy never recovered any wreckage or remains from the five aircraft in Flight 19 or a flying boat that disappeared on December 5, 1945.
content:
U.S. Navy Lt. Charles Carroll Taylor served in the Pacific in World War II. He survived the deadliest war in world history, only to find himself battling to survive three months after the Japanese surrendered.

On December 5, 1945, Taylor led five Grumman TBM Avenger torpedo bombers—collectively known as Flight 19—during a training run. They left Naval Air Station Fort Lauderdale shortly after 2 p.m. local time but never returned. The increasingly frantic Taylor sent his last radio message more than four hours after takeoff.

“All planes close up tight… we’ll have to ditch unless landfall… when the first plane drops below 10 gallons, we all go down together,” Taylor told the other 13 service members on Flight 19.

Also Read: The enduring mystery of a Navy ship that sank in the Bermuda Triangle

Search-and-rescue teams never found their remains, any wreckage, or any indication on the water’s surface of where they went down. It was a horrific outcome, made all the more tragic when a Navy flying boat assigned to search for Flight 19 also went down. Thirteen more people died in that accident, bringing the total number of lives lost that day to 27. 

“I Don’t Know How to Get to Fort Lauderdale”

The planes of Flight 19 were to leave their base in South Florida, then drop practice bombs near Bimini in the Bahamas. After that, they were supposed to fly over Grand Bahama Island before heading back to Fort Lauderdale.

Three crew members each manned four of the five Avengers, with two on the other bomber. Some of the service members were trainee pilots. Everything was OK up until the time that they released their practice ordnance. Shortly after, Taylor believed the compasses on his aircraft were not operational, leaving him basically to fly blind.

“I am sure I’m in the Keys, but I don’t know how far down and I don’t know how to get to Fort Lauderdale,” Taylor radioed.

Lt. Robert F. Cox, a Navy flight instructor, overheard Taylor’s pleas and relayed them to the Naval Air Station. Cox also asked the Avengers whether he could help.

There was not much he could do, because the service members on Flight 19 had no idea exactly where they were. As each minute passed, heightened levels of desperation gripped those inside the Avengers.

At least one became exasperated with Taylor, because the Avengers were heading east instead of west. Perhaps part of that frustration stemmed from Taylor’s unfamiliarity with the area. Taylor, who came from NAS Miami, had experience flying over the Florida Keys but not the Bahamas.

As nighttime approached, normal protocol would be for the planes to head in the direction of the setting sun. Apparently believing flying west would take them over the Gulf of Mexico and away from their base, Taylor had the planes heading on the wrong course.

“Dammit, if we could just fly west, we would get home,” one service member implored. “Head west, dammit.” 

The Rescue Efforts

Taylor eventually relented, but he changed his mind again. Amid the confusion, the Avengers were running out of fuel. With the planes of Flight 19 lost, their efforts were made more difficult, because the weather began to worsen.

As their situation became more dire, service members on Flight 19 sent other radio transmissions. On one, a voice was heard saying they were unsure which way to go. “Everything looks strange, even the ocean,” he exclaimed.

Another message, according to the U.S. Naval History and Heritage Command, highlighted their desperation.

“We can’t tell where we are… everything is… can’t make out anything,” the pilot said. “We think we may be about 225 miles northeast of base.”

In response to the emergency, the Navy diverted two PBM Mariner flying boats to Flight 19’s last estimated location. Those seaplanes didn’t have the best reputation for safety. The PBM Mariners became known as “flying gas tanks” because they were susceptible to catching fire.

Radio contact was lost with one of the PBM Mariners early in the search for Flight 19. It is believed an explosion destroyed the flying boat. It was a conclusion reinforced by a nearby merchant vessel reporting “a burst of flame” in the area where the PBM Mariner was.

Once the sun rose on December 6, the Navy intensified its search for the downed aircraft. The search, which also involved the Coast Guard, lasted five days. Three hundred-plus boats and aircraft covered approximately 300,000 square miles but didn’t turn up anything.

“The Lost Patrol”
